ARI.name: Cardinals
ARI.campOpens: Veterans fully reported July 22, 2026 at State Farm Stadium (Glendale); first practice July 24. Arizona and Carolina were the first two teams to report because they play the Aug. 6 Hall of Fame Game.
ARI.biggestUnknown: Whether the quarterback position is functional at all. The depth chart is settled — Brissett's $15.5M guarantee decided that — but he went 1-11 as a starter in 2025, Kyler Murray was released in March, and the fallback options are Gardner Minshew and rookie Carson Beck. Nothing else on this roster carries that much unresolved variance.

battles.why: Adams is the incumbent (694 snaps, 11 starts at RG last year) but the Cardinals spent a 2026 second-round pick on Bisontis, and Adams' offseason arrest on gun charges in Canada clouded his standing.
battles.stakes: The last unsettled spot on an offensive line that has to protect a stopgap QB and open lanes for the No. 3 overall pick, in Mike LaFleur's first year running the offense.
battles.money: Bisontis is a 2026 second-round pick on a fully guaranteed rookie deal; Adams is a 2024 third-rounder in year three with no guarantees left worth protecting. Second-round capital plus an off-field legal issue on the incumbent tilts this toward the rookie, but Adams did enter camp taking first-team work.

ATL.name: Falcons
ATL.campOpens: Rookies reported Friday, July 24; veterans report Tuesday, July 28; first full-squad practice Wednesday, July 29 at the team facility in Flowery Branch, GA (camp runs through Aug. 26; 12 open practices July 31–Aug. 20)
ATL.biggestUnknown: Michael Penix Jr.'s knee. Everything downstream — whether the QB competition is real or ceremonial, whether Tagovailoa is a bridge or the starter, and whether the new Stefanski/Cunningham regime spends 2026 evaluating Penix or shopping for a 2027 quarterback — depends on how much a player coming off ACL surgery can actually do in August. There is no reporting that resolves it.

battles.why: An entirely new football operation — HC Kevin Stefanski, GM Ian Cunningham, team president Matt Ryan — has no institutional attachment to Penix, who is rehabbing a torn ACL, and it added Tagovailoa in March on a throwaway contract.
battles.stakes: Decides whether 2026 is a bridge/evaluation year or the season Penix's No. 8 overall selection is validated, and it sets up the franchise's 2027 QB decision.
battles.money: Tagovailoa signed a one-year deal worth roughly $1.3M — essentially the minimum — because Miami still owes him $54M guaranteed for 2026 after releasing him, so Atlanta carries no financial obligation to play him. Penix's leverage is draft capital (No. 8 overall, 2024) held by a previous regime, which is the weakest form of protection there is. Neither man is protected by money, which is exactly why this one is real. Health, not merit, may settle it: reporting has Tagovailoa favored for Week 1 mainly because Penix is still working back from ACL surgery.

battles.stakes: Special-teams snaps and injury insurance behind London; also the depth that determines whether Atlanta can run three-WR sets without a drop-off.
battles.money: Every contender is a UDFA, practice-squad graduate or UFL signing with no guaranteed money. The new coaching staff explicitly has no prior attachments here, which removes the usual thumb on the scale for perennial camp standouts Blair and Drummond.

battles.stakes: Realistically this is a swing-tackle and depth battle, not a starting job — the actual competition is Morris vs. Jerrell vs. Nelson for backup tackle and practice-squad spots.

BAL.name: Ravens
BAL.campOpens: Rookies, QBs and injured veterans reported July 24; veterans report July 28, 2026. First public practice July 29 at the Under Armour Performance Center in Owings Mills; camp runs through Aug. 17.
BAL.biggestUnknown: The starting center. Baltimore let a three-time Pro Bowl center walk, went most of the offseason without a real answer, and then patched it with a 1-year, $3M veteran who was medically cleared from a torn Achilles days before camp. Every other unsettled spot on this roster is a rotation or depth question; this one is a Week 1 starting job in front of Lamar Jackson in a first-year offensive scheme, with no fallback who has ever started a season opener.

battles.why: Three-time Pro Bowler Tyler Linderbaum left for the Raiders in free agency and Baltimore did not replace him until signing Pocic 12 days before the first practice, leaving a genuinely open starting job with a health caveat.
battles.stakes: The pivot in front of Lamar Jackson in Declan Doyle's brand-new offense; a bad answer here undercuts the whole scheme installation and the interior line rebuild around John Simpson and rookie Vega Ioane.
battles.money: Pocic is on a 1-year, $3M deal with $1.5M in incentives — nowhere near enough guaranteed money to hand him the job, and he was only medically cleared from a Dec. 7 torn left Achilles shortly before camp. He has 97 career starts; of Pinter, Gwyn and Bullock only Pinter has ever started an NFL game (never in Week 1, never more than three in a season). Pocic is the clear favorite on résumé, not on money.

battles.why: Baltimore signed no veteran receiver this offseason and instead drafted two, so everything behind Zay Flowers and Rashod Bateman is up for grabs in a new offensive system.
battles.stakes: Jackson's third and fourth options in Doyle's offense, and whether the Ravens' decision to solve receiver purely through the draft actually works.
battles.money: Flowers (2023 first-rounder) and Bateman (signed a multi-year extension in 2025) are locked starters and are not competing. Draft capital tilts the back end: Ja'Kobi Lane went in Round 3 (No. 80) and Elijah Sarratt in Round 4 (No. 115), which makes both very likely to make the 53 regardless of camp. The genuinely at-risk players are Wester and Wade. Walker, entering year three, is the incumbent favorite for WR3 but has no contractual protection.

BUF.name: Bills
BUF.campOpens: Rookies reported July 21, 2026; veterans reported July 28; first full practice Wednesday, July 29 at St. John Fisher University in Pittsford, NY. Seven public Pittsford practices run July 29 - Aug. 7 (all 8:30 a.m.), plus an added public session at the new stadium.
BUF.biggestUnknown: Whether the defense actually functions in Jim Leonhard's 3-4. Buffalo ran McDermott's scheme for nine years and is now rebuilding the front seven from scratch with a first-year head coach, a converted 3-4 front, unproven 2025 draftees (T.J. Sanders, Landon Jackson) coming off lost rookie seasons, and position switches (Joey Bosa moving on the front). Three of the five camp battles above are downstream of that one question — until the scheme takes, no defensive depth chart on this roster means much.

battles.why: The switch to Jim Leonhard's 3-4 raises the value of the second off-ball linebacker, and Williams — who had the job to lose — was hurt this offseason, opening the door for the rookie.
battles.stakes: A full-time defensive starter in a brand-new scheme; whoever wins is on the field for the majority of base snaps in a defense with no returning identity.
battles.money: Williams is a 2023 third-round pick now at the end of his rookie deal, so there is no guaranteed money protecting him. Elarms-Orr is a 2026 fourth-rounder — real but not decisive capital. Brady said Williams should be ready by the start of camp, which keeps this a true two-man race rather than a default handoff.
battles.reportedAs: ILB2 (inside linebacker next to Terrel Bernard)

battles.why: Hairston's rookie year was wrecked by injuries, so beat writers frame the job as re-openable, and Buffalo drafted Igbinosun out of Ohio State to add competition.
battles.stakes: A full-time starting outside corner in a new coverage scheme, on a defense with essentially no continuity.
battles.money: Hairston was Buffalo's 2025 first-round pick (No. 30) on a fully guaranteed four-year rookie contract with a fifth-year option — first-round corners in year two effectively never lose camp jobs to a rookie. Brandon Beane said publicly after the 2026 draft that Benford and Hairston are penciled in as the boundary starters. Treat the 'battle' as real pressure on Hairston's snap count, not a real threat to the starting job unless he is hurt again. (I could not confirm Igbinosun's exact draft round — Buffalo's 2026 second-rounder went to Chicago in the DJ Moore trade, so some outlets' 'second-round rookie' label is suspect.)

battles.stakes: The last starting job on a defensive front that has to justify the entire scheme change; it also determines whether Buffalo's 2025 defensive line draft class was worth it.
battles.money: Sanders enters ahead on capital — Buffalo traded up to No. 41 in 2025 to get him — but he lost his rookie year to a knee injury (IR in October), so this is effectively his first real camp and the tape does not back the capital yet. Landon Jackson (2025 third round) also lost his rookie season to a knee injury and, per local reporting, is not even guaranteed a 2026 roster spot. Durant is the cheapest of the three. Draft capital tilts this toward Sanders but has not settled it.

CAR.name: Panthers
CAR.campOpens: Veterans reported Wednesday, July 22, 2026 — Carolina and Arizona were the first two teams to fully report, because both play in the Hall of Fame Game on Aug. 6. Camp runs July 22 through Aug. 28 at Bank of America Stadium in uptown Charlotte.
CAR.biggestUnknown: The left side of the offensive line. Ikem Ekwonu's return from a ruptured patellar tendon has no timeline at all, the Panthers spent both a first-round pick (Freeling) and a free-agent contract (Walker) on the same position without declaring a winner, and the center next to them is an open competition between a one-year veteran and a fifth-round rookie. Two of the five OL spots have no settled answer eight weeks from Week 1.

battles.why: Ikem Ekwonu ruptured his patellar tendon in the playoff game with no return timeline, so the Panthers signed Walker in free agency and then took Freeling at No. 19 overall — two solutions to the same hole.
battles.stakes: It is Bryce Young's blindside in a season where the front office has bet its jobs on Young taking a step forward; get it wrong and the whole offense is compromised.
battles.money: Walker signed 1 yr / $10M but structured as only ~$4M base plus $6M in incentives — very little dead money if he loses the job. Freeling is the No. 19 overall pick on a 4 yr / $20.9M deal with an $11.6M signing bonus. The draft capital points to Freeling eventually; the reps right now point to Walker.

CHI.name: Bears
CHI.campOpens: Rookies reported Saturday, July 25, 2026; veterans report Tuesday, July 28, 2026. First practice July 29, first fan-open practice July 31, at Halas Hall (Lake Forest, IL).
CHI.biggestUnknown: The interior and left edge of the offensive line. Drew Dalman retired in the spring and Ozzy Trapilo tore a patellar tendon in the playoffs, so the two spots the Bears thought were settled in January are the two they're rebuilding in July — a traded-for veteran center or a rookie second-rounder snapping the ball, and a left tackle on a one-year prove-it deal with a durability history. Everything about Caleb Williams' year-three leap depends on how those two spots resolve, and neither has a contract or a draft pick large enough to have pre-decided it.

battles.why: DJ Moore was traded to Buffalo, leaving a vacancy behind Rome Odunze and Luther Burden III with no established third option on the roster.
battles.stakes: Determines who gets the No. 3 target share in a Ben Johnson offense that historically feeds a movable slot/gadget receiver, plus the return job.
battles.money: No meaningful guaranteed money or draft capital in the room — Raymond is a veteran special-teams signing and Thomas a late-round rookie, so this is decided on merit. Raymond's edge is scheme familiarity: he played for Ben Johnson in Detroit from 2022-24, which is a real thumb on the scale in a first-team-reps sense. Caveat: 'WR3' here mostly means return man plus 25-30 snaps a game, not a fantasy-relevant role.

battles.why: Ozzy Trapilo, the presumed 2026 starter, tore a patellar tendon in the playoffs, forcing the Bears to re-open the job and re-sign Braxton Jones.
battles.stakes: Caleb Williams' blind side. If Jones' health holds this is a non-issue; if it doesn't, the Bears are down to two players who haven't taken meaningful LT snaps in over a year.
battles.money: Jones was re-signed to a one-year, $5M deal specifically to be the starter and took every first-team rep in the spring with a clean bill of health and 44 career starts. Wills and Amegadjie (2024 3rd round) are not locks to even make the 53. Treat national 'wide-open left tackle race' framing skeptically — some of it is recycled 2025 copy that still lists Trapilo as an active competitor. The real question here is Jones' durability, not the depth chart.

CIN.name: Bengals
CIN.campOpens: Rookies reported Saturday, July 25, 2026; veterans report Tuesday, July 28, with the first full practice Wednesday, July 29 (Paycor Stadium / Kettering Health Practice Fields, Cincinnati).
CIN.biggestUnknown: Whether the post-Hendrickson pass rush is actually a pass rush. The Bengals replaced a four-time Pro Bowler with Boye Mafe plus a pile of unproven draft capital, and the single biggest variable is Shemar Stewart — a 2025 top-20 pick whose rookie year was consumed by a contract holdout and then a knee injury, leaving the team with essentially no evidence about a player it needs to be a starter.

battles.why: The Bengals spent a 2026 fourth-rounder on Lew and Karras is 33 and in the final year of his deal, so the succession question is live even if this season's answer is not.
battles.stakes: Karras has been the most consistent piece of Burrow's protection for four years; the Bengals return all five 2025 starters and continuity is the entire premise of the 2026 line.
battles.money: Karras is the incumbent starter and the Bengals publicly framed 2026 as bringing back all five starting linemen — the first time in the Burrow era. Lew is coming off a torn ACL at Auburn and only just avoided a camp-opening injury list; fourth-round capital does not unseat a proven starter in August. Read Lew as the 2027 starter and this camp as a redshirt-with-reps, not a battle.

CLE.name: Browns
CLE.campOpens: Rookies reported July 23, 2026; veterans report Tuesday, July 28, 2026, with the first practice July 29. Camp runs July 28-Aug. 25 at the CrossCountry Mortgage Campus in Berea, Ohio.
CLE.biggestUnknown: Whether Deshaun Watson can physically still play NFL football. He has not taken a snap since Oct. 20, 2024 after two torn Achilles, and no amount of spring 7-on-7 answers it — everything about Cleveland's 2026 offense, and by extension the evaluation of Shedeur Sanders, hangs on what the first week of padded practice reveals.

battles.why: David Njoku is gone and the Browns flooded the room — signed Stoll, re-signed Whiteheart, tendered Bates, and drafted two tight ends — without establishing a clear No. 2.
battles.stakes: Njoku's vacated snaps and target share have to go somewhere; whoever wins this decides whether Cleveland runs more 12 personnel or funnels everything through Fannin.
battles.money: No meaningful money or capital anywhere in the group — Stoll is a veteran-minimum blocking specialist, Royer a mid/late-round rookie, Carsen Ryan a seventh-rounder. Nothing here is pre-decided. Fannin himself is untouchable after leading the team with 72 catches as a rookie.

DAL.name: Cowboys
DAL.campOpens: Veterans and rookies reported to Oxnard, CA on Tue July 28, 2026; opening press conference and first practice Wed July 29; first padded practice Mon Aug 3; Oxnard portion ends Aug 18 before the team returns to Ford Center at The Star in Frisco
DAL.biggestUnknown: Whether first-year coordinator Christian Parker's 3-4 defense — with as many as seven new starters, a rookie first-rounder at safety, and an unsettled off-ball linebacker room — can be functional by September. Everything else on this roster is a depth question; the defense is a structural one.

battles.why: CeeDee Lamb, George Pickens, and Jake Ferguson are locked, so the fight is purely for the last skill-position spots. UDFA Michael Trigg has generated real buzz at TE3, and Mingo is fighting for the fifth WR job against 2026 draftee Anthony Smith.
battles.stakes: Special-teams value and injury insurance for the league's most top-heavy skill group; also whether Dallas finally cuts bait on a former Day 2 tight end.
battles.money: Schoonmaker is 2023 second-round capital, but that capital is now three years old and near the end of its rookie deal — the point at which it stops protecting a player. Mingo cost Dallas a Day 2-ish trade asset, which is the main thing keeping him on the roster. Smith is 2026 late-round capital.

battles.why: Repeatedly described by beat coverage as the most questionable room on the roster: Overshown has a serious injury history, Winters was acquired in a trade from San Francisco rather than paid as a lock, and third-round rookie Barham is converting from a college edge/hybrid role into a full-time off-ball job in Christian Parker's new 3-4.
battles.stakes: The green-dot communicator in a first-year scheme installing up to seven new defensive starters — this is the position most likely to determine whether a defense that allowed a league-worst 30 PPG in 2025 actually improves.
battles.money: No one here has meaningful guaranteed money. Barham is 2026 third-round capital (real but not decisive); Winters arrived by trade on a modest deal; Overshown's leverage is entirely health-dependent.

battles.why: Bland is the only locked starter (and has a nagging foot issue that has cost him games in each of the last two seasons). Revel gets his first healthy NFL offseason in Year 2, Durant was signed in the first week of free agency, and Dallas kept stacking bodies at the position through the draft and into July.
battles.stakes: With Caleb Downs taking slot reps, whoever wins the outside job opposite Bland plays close to every snap; the loser becomes expensive depth on a defense that gets tested deep.
battles.money: Durant's free-agent deal gives him a floor, and Revel carries 2025 third-round capital, but neither has the kind of guarantee that ends a competition. Kendrick is on a one-year deal and is a genuine cut candidate. Moore is 2026 fourth-round capital — depth, not a mandate.

battles.why: Brian Schottenheimer publicly opened it — 'Tyler's biggest thing is the consistency has not been there,' and 'we're going to make Tyler earn it' — after Dallas cycled through three left tackles in 2025.
battles.stakes: Protecting Dak Prescott's blind side on a line that ranked 19th in pass block win rate in 2025; it is the offense's one soft spot next to Lamb/Pickens.
battles.money: Guyton is the 2024 first-round pick (No. 29) on a fully guaranteed rookie deal with a fifth-year option decision coming — teams essentially never bench that in camp. Jon Machota (The Athletic) reported Guyton took all the first-team reps through minicamp and remains the 'clear favorite.' Thomas was drafted 204 picks later; Shelton is a developmental 2026 fourth-rounder. The competition is real as motivation, not as an outcome.

DEN.name: Broncos
DEN.campOpens: Veterans report Tuesday, July 28, 2026 (rookies reported July 22); camp runs through Aug. 19 at the team facility in Englewood, CO
DEN.biggestUnknown: Whether the passing offense actually works in its new configuration — Bo Nix coming off a broken ankle, a first-time play-caller in new OC Davis Webb, and a brand-new WR1 in Jaylen Waddle. No roster spot on this team is as unsettled as the question of what this offense is, and none of it will be resolved by a camp depth chart.

battles.why: Powers is on an expiring deal with two younger, cheaper alternatives on the roster, so the media has framed camp as a three-way competition.
battles.stakes: If a young player wins it, Denver clears a large 2026 cap number and settles its interior line for years; if not, it's the status quo with a lame-duck starter.
battles.money: This is the one to be skeptical of. Mike Klis (9News) reported Denver made a final decision on Powers: no trade, no release, no pay cut — same team, same job, same pay — despite reporting that cutting him would have saved roughly $12.7M. A team that declines an eight-figure saving in the spring is not planning to bench the player in August. Palczewski (new three-year deal) and Casey (2026 fourth-rounder) are the succession plan for 2027, not the 2026 Week 1 starters.

DET.name: Lions
DET.campOpens: Rookies reported July 25, 2026; veterans report Tuesday July 28; first full practice expected Wednesday July 29 in Allen Park. Notably, Dan Campbell has announced the Lions will hold NO joint practices in 2026, so every evaluation rep happens in-house or in preseason games.
DET.biggestUnknown: The secondary. Detroit lost its 2024 first-round corner (Terrion Arnold) to a felony arrest and release on June 29 with no replacement plan, opens camp with All-Pro safety Kerby Joseph and star nickel Brian Branch (Achilles) both on PUP, and its one settled outside corner, D.J. Reed, is coming off an injury-shortened season and has not been tested with pads on. Every other battle on this roster is known, healthy candidates competing under normal conditions. This one is a hole with a timeline nobody can give you, landing exactly as Kelvin Sheppard tries to install a more nickel-heavy, matchup-driven scheme that requires the defensive backs he doesn't currently have on the field.

battles.why: Kalif Raymond's departure opened the slot/return utility role, and Detroit added four UFL receivers to the 90-man to compete for the back of the room.
battles.stakes: Low individually, real cumulatively - these spots are decided as much by Dave Fipp's special teams needs as by receiving ability, and they determine whether Detroit can carry an extra body elsewhere.
battles.money: Important framing correction: the WR3 job is NOT open, whatever gets written. Amon-Ra St. Brown and Jameson Williams (back-to-back 1,000-yard seasons) are locked at 1 and 2, and Isaac TeSlaa took hold of WR3 late in his rookie year with six touchdowns. Dortch was signed with prior familiarity in Petzing's scheme, making him the favorite for the Raymond role. Anyone selling a 'Lions WR3 battle' is manufacturing it.

battles.why: Mahogany is the incumbent, but Detroit deliberately stacked the room in free agency because his 2025 play didn't settle the spot; beat coverage frames it as him needing to show real improvement to hold off two additions.
battles.stakes: Combined with the RT opening, Detroit could start two brand-new offensive line pieces in front of a 31-year-old Goff behind a brand-new play-caller.
battles.money: The cleanest genuinely open job on the roster, because nobody is financially or positionally protected: Mahogany is a 2024 sixth-round pick (no capital shield), Bartch and Scruggs are both journeyman-priced veterans. One wrinkle that matters: Bartch sat out the entire offseason program rehabbing an injury, so he enters behind on reps despite being seen as the top challenger. Scruggs' three-position interior versatility may make him more valuable as a swing backup than as a starter.

battles.why: Taylor Decker was released this offseason and Penei Sewell slid to left tackle, vacating right tackle entirely; the Lions then spent the No. 17 pick on Miller and signed Borom in free agency the same spring.
battles.stakes: The only starting spot on the line in front of Jared Goff with no incumbent, being sorted under a first-year offensive coordinator (Drew Petzing) with no joint practices to stress-test it.
battles.money: Real competition in July, but the thumb is on the scale. Miller is the No. 17 overall pick, signed, and the team released Decker to make this configuration possible. Borom's 1-year, $5M deal (~$4.90M guaranteed) is swing-tackle insurance pricing - enough to make him a credible Week 1 answer if Miller stumbles, not enough to hold the job all season against first-round capital. Expect Borom to win reps and Miller to win the season.

battles.why: Terrion Arnold, the 2024 first-round pick penciled in as the Week 1 starter, was released June 29 after being arrested on eight felony counts (four robbery-with-a-firearm, four kidnapping) tied to a February armed robbery in Tampa - an opening created six weeks before camp with no planned successor.
battles.stakes: Kerby Joseph and Brian Branch (Achilles) both open camp on PUP and D.J. Reed is coming off injury; if CB2 is a hole, Kelvin Sheppard's shift toward more nickel and matchup-driven coverage is dead on arrival.
battles.money: Nobody here is protected. Ya-Sin re-signed on a 1-year deal reported in the $3.2M-$4M range with roughly $2.64M guaranteed - rotational/CB3 pricing, not a locked starting job. Rakestraw carries the most draft capital left in the room (2024 second-rounder) but has barely played. Arnold's release removed the only real capital argument on the roster.

HOU.name: Texans
HOU.campOpens: Veterans and rookies report Tuesday, July 28, 2026; first practice Wednesday, July 29, at the Houston Methodist Training Center. Eight practices are free and open to fans (Aug 1, 3, 4, 5, 7, 8, 10, 18).
HOU.biggestUnknown: Whether Keylan Rutledge can actually play center in the NFL. He took 98.3% of his college snaps at right guard, and the entire interior configuration — center, left guard, and where Wyatt Teller ends up — cascades off that one question. Houston has now rebuilt this line in three straight offseasons without solving it.

battles.why: Dell has not practiced in roughly 18 months since his 2024 leg injury and missed all of 2025, leaving the third receiver job behind Nico Collins and Jayden Higgins genuinely unclaimed.
battles.stakes: Who gets the volume in three-receiver sets in an offense that has to prove 2025's passing-game collapse was situational.
battles.money: Noel is a 2025 third-round pick and Higgins a 2025 second-rounder, so the future capital sits with the sophomores. Dell's rookie deal carries no meaningful guarantee leverage, and he has already been floated externally as a trade candidate — his contract will not save the job for him.

battles.why: Houston traded up for a first-round guard and immediately put him on first-team center reps in the spring despite him never having snapped in a real game; Andrews started all 17 in 2025 but was a weak link.
battles.stakes: Determines whether the interior OL that undermined C.J. Stroud in 2025 is actually fixed, and whether Houston's first-round pick plays his natural position or a learned one.
battles.money: Rutledge was the No. 26 overall pick (Houston traded up two spots) on a four-year, $19.276M fully guaranteed rookie deal. That capital means Rutledge starts *somewhere* almost regardless of camp; what is genuinely open is whether it's center or guard. Andrews is cheap depth with no guarantees protecting him.

battles.why: Teller was acquired to start but is a career right guard being asked to flip sides for the first time since his rookie year; Ingram is locked in at RG on a new extension, so the only interior slot in play is left.
battles.stakes: The left side in front of Stroud's blind side, paired with second-year LT Aireontae Ersery.
battles.money: Teller is a former All-Pro Houston traded for this offseason and Ingram signed an extension before the draft — both are paid to start. Teams do not trade for and pay a two-time All-Pro guard to lose a camp battle. The realistic outcome is Teller at LG and Rutledge sorted into C or a swing role.

battles.money: Neither player has draft capital or guaranteed money protecting him — Robinson is a low-cost veteran addition with a career high of 1.5 sacks, Byrd a 2024 seventh-rounder. This is one of the few Texans jobs where the depth chart is genuinely blank.

IND.name: Colts
IND.campOpens: Rookies reported Monday, July 27, 2026; veterans reported Tuesday, July 28; first full practice Wednesday, July 29 at Grand Park Sports Campus, Westfield, IN (camp runs through August 20).
IND.biggestUnknown: Daniel Jones' Achilles. He says he is "a full go" for the first practice and expects to be in 11-on-11 immediately, and he did seven-on-sevens by the end of the offseason program — but he tore it in early December and the Colts just committed two years and $88M to him on that basis. Nothing else on this roster is close: a functioning Jones makes the Colts a playoff team with an open kicker job as their biggest problem, and a compromised one hands the season to Anthony Richardson or a sixth-round rookie. Camp practices won't answer it; Week 8 will.

battles.why: Shrader was 13-of-14 before tearing his ACL and MCL in Week 5 of 2025; Grupe replaced him and went 11-of-11 including a franchise-record 60-yarder. Neither man lost the job.
battles.stakes: Whoever loses is likely another team's starting kicker, and the Colts have been churning kickers for years — this is the rare specialist battle with actual league-wide value on both sides.
battles.money: Both are on cheap one-year deals (Grupe re-signed in March, Shrader is on a minimum-ish deal coming off surgery). There is no guaranteed money anywhere to tilt it. Shrader is the nominal leader only because of health timeline, not contract.

battles.why: Michael Pittman Jr. was traded to Pittsburgh, vacating a large target share behind Alec Pierce and Josh Downs.
battles.stakes: Determines whether the Colts play meaningful 11 personnel or lean harder on tight ends and Jonathan Taylor; Pierce's new deal assumes real WR help exists.
battles.money: Alec Pierce's four-year, $116M deal and Josh Downs' role lock the top two, so this is strictly for the third spot. Dulin has the inside track on reputation and special-teams value, not money — he is a career special-teamer, not a protected investment. Burks is a 2026 draft pick but a mid/late-round one, so no capital settles it.

JAX.name: Jaguars
JAX.campOpens: Rookies and quarterbacks reported July 25, 2026; veterans report July 28; first practice July 29 at the Miller Electric Center, camp running through August 26.
JAX.biggestUnknown: Travis Hunter's two-way workload. The Jaguars have said repeatedly he is the No. 1 cornerback, but the offensive half is genuinely undecided — he played 67% of snaps before an LCL tear ended his rookie year after seven games, the team then spent two of its 2026 picks on tight ends (Nate Boerkircher in Rd 2, Tanner Koziol in Rd 5), and Coen's scheme leans heavier personnel. Nobody, including the staff, has said how many offensive snaps he gets, and that single number moves the projection for the entire receiver room.

battles.why: Travis Etienne left for New Orleans and the Jaguars deliberately replaced him in the aggregate rather than with one back; Tuten had the whole offseason as the No. 1 while Rodriguez was sidelined for most of the workouts.
battles.stakes: Whether Jacksonville can run the ball at all after letting its lead back walk, and a large fantasy/usage question — this is a true committee unless someone separates.
battles.money: Rodriguez signed two years, $10M ($12M max) with $6.2M fully guaranteed — that guarantees him a roster spot and real touches, but it is not lead-back money. Tuten is a 2025 Day 3 pick on a rookie deal, so no contract fact decides this; Coen has publicly hyped Tuten for 'a big year,' which is the strongest signal in the room.

battles.why: Mekari was a disappointment in year one in Jacksonville (missed three games, ranked near the bottom of qualifying guards in run-blocking efficiency) and the team spent a 2025 third-rounder on Milum, who is finally healthy after a camp knee injury wiped out his rookie summer.
battles.stakes: Trevor Lawrence's interior protection and the run game in Liam Coen's second year; it is the only starting spot on the line where the incumbent has clearly underperformed his price.
battles.money: Mekari signed a three-year, $37.5M deal in March 2025, which is the argument for him keeping the job — but he also has swing-tackle value, so the Jaguars can bench him at guard without eating the contract as a pure loss. Milum (2025 Rd 3) and Pregnon (2026 Rd 3, No. 88) are both cheap draft capital pushing him.

KC.name: Chiefs
KC.campOpens: Rookies and QBs reported Fri July 24; veterans reported July 28; camp runs July 28/29 through Aug 20 at Missouri Western State University, St. Joseph, MO (16th year there). First open practice July 29 (season-ticket holders only).
KC.biggestUnknown: Patrick Mahomes' left knee. He tore the ACL and LCL in Week 15 against the Chargers, and although Andy Reid cleared him for full participation and he opened camp in a brace without incident, nobody — including the Chiefs — knows how much of his off-platform, extend-the-play movement comes back by the Week 1 opener at Denver on Sept. 14. Every other question on this roster is downstream of that one.

battles.why: Kansas City traded up to No. 6 for Mansoor Delane to lock one boundary spot, then stacked three plausible veterans/young starters on the other side with no incumbent clearly established.
battles.stakes: Spagnuolo's man-heavy pressure looks require two corners who can survive alone; this is the difference between blitzing freely and playing scared.
battles.money: Delane (No. 6 overall, highest KC pick since 2013) is untouchable — the battle is only for the spot opposite him. Sneed is a re-signed veteran on a reset deal rather than the big-money contract he had in Tennessee, so none of the three has a guarantee large enough to decide it; ESPN's Nate Taylor has flagged this as camp's top competition.

battles.why: Chamarri Conner is moving from nickel back to safety to replace Bryan Cook (lost in free agency), vacating the slot outright.
battles.stakes: KC plays nickel as its base personnel; whoever wins is effectively a starter, and the loser of the safety domino makes it worse if Conner struggles.
battles.money: Kohou signed as a free agent coming off an ACL tear — a modest prove-it deal, not a contract that guarantees snaps. Canady is a 2026 fourth-rounder: enough capital to get a long look, not enough to be handed the job.

LV.name: Raiders
LV.campOpens: Rookies reported Thursday, July 23; veterans report Tuesday, July 28, with the first practice Wednesday, July 29. Camp runs July 29-Aug. 29 at the Intermountain Health Performance Center in Henderson, Nev.
LV.biggestUnknown: Not who starts Week 1, but when the Cousins-to-Mendoza handoff happens. Cousins' $20M guarantee and Kubiak's public statements settle the opener; nothing about the trigger for benching a fully guaranteed veteran for the No. 1 overall pick has been established, and every other roster decision (OL continuity, WR usage, how aggressive the play-calling gets) bends around that unannounced date.

battles.why: Signing Tyler Linderbaum locked center and pushed 2024 second-rounder Jackson Powers-Johnson out to guard, leaving one interior spot with four bodies and no incumbent; Burford took most first-team reps in the offseason program but Rogers reportedly pushed him hard.
battles.stakes: The last unsettled spot on a line rebuilt to protect a 37-year-old pocket QB now and a No. 1 overall pick later — continuity here is the difference between Kubiak's play-action offense working and not.
battles.money: Powers-Johnson (2024 No. 44) and Linderbaum are locked by capital/contract, so the battle is only for the other guard. Burford is a low-cost veteran with no meaningful guarantee; Rogers is a 2025 third-round pick. Nobody in this group has money that decides it.
battles.reportedAs: LG (the guard spot next to Jackson Powers-Johnson)

LAC.name: Chargers
LAC.campOpens: Rookies reported July 23, 2026; full squad/first camp practice July 29, 2026 at The Bolt in El Segundo, CA (camp runs through late August)
LAC.biggestUnknown: Whether the completely rebuilt offensive interior holds up in Mike McDaniel's brand-new offense — the left guard spot is unfilled, Biadasz and Strange are first-year additions at center and right guard, and both bookends (Rashawn Slater, torn patellar tendon in last year's camp; Joe Alt, ankle) are returning from season-ending injuries. Everything about the 2026 Chargers offense is downstream of that.

battles.why: The top three receivers are set, but the back end of the room is unsettled and the return job was openly rotated in minicamp among Hampton, Mitchell, Vidal, Ross and Jackson.
battles.stakes: McDaniel's scheme needs more than three usable receivers, and return duty is often the tiebreaker for the last one or two WR/RB roster spots.
battles.money: Brenen Thompson is a 2026 fourth-rounder with the fastest 40 at the Combine, which gives him a leg up but not a lock; Derius Davis is a returner-first incumbent with no guaranteed money protecting him. Keaton Mitchell is a cheap FA add brought in to replace Najee Harris's early-down role and is competing with tendered ERFA Kimani Vidal (643 rush yards in 2025) for the RB2 job behind Omarion Hampton.

battles.why: It is the only genuinely open starting job on the roster — Slater and Alt return at tackle, Tyler Biadasz was signed to start at center and Cole Strange at right guard, leaving LG as the one unfilled spot after a heavy OL investment offseason.
battles.stakes: It is the last hole in a line that has to keep Justin Herbert upright in Mike McDaniel's first year running the offense, with both starting tackles coming off season-ending injuries.
battles.money: Slaughter was the No. 63 pick (2nd round, 2026) — real but not overwhelming draft capital, and he has not played guard since high school after starring at center at Florida. Awosika is a cheap veteran FA signing (11 career starts in Detroit) and Penning is a re-signed swing lineman working with the third team. No one here has guaranteed money large enough to decide it, which is exactly why it is open. Awosika led in the spring; McDaniel said he would not really evaluate it until the pads come on, and Harbaugh in mid-June called the competition "raging on."

LA.campOpens: Veterans reported Saturday, July 25, 2026; on-field camp runs July 26 – Aug. 7 at Loyola Marymount University in Los Angeles.
LA.biggestUnknown: The quarterback room behind Matthew Stafford. Stafford is the reigning MVP but is on a deliberately limited camp rep plan and sat out the first practice, so the Rams genuinely do not know yet whether Ty Simpson (No. 13 overall) is ready to be the emergency answer in 2026 or whether Stetson Bennett is still the safer hand — and reporting from OTAs suggested neither has seized it. Everything else on this roster is depth-tier; this is the only unsettled thing that could decide the season.

battles.why: Davante Adams and Puka Nacua are locked in as the top two, and the No. 3 job behind them is unclaimed — sources disagree on whether it's Whittington/Smith or the two young draftees, which is itself evidence nobody has won it.
battles.stakes: McVay's offense runs heavy 11 personnel, so WR3 is close to a starter's snap count; it also determines whether a fifth receiver survives the 53-man cut.
battles.money: No meaningful money or draft capital anywhere in the group — Mumpfield was a 2025 seventh-rounder, Daniels a 2026 sixth-rounder, Whittington a 2024 sixth-rounder. Nothing is protecting any of them, which is exactly why it is open. Mumpfield is a real cut candidate if the Rams keep only five WRs.

MIA.name: Dolphins
MIA.campOpens: Rookies reported July 21, 2026; veterans report Tuesday, July 28, 2026. Camp runs July 28 through Aug. 26 at the Baptist Health Training Complex in Miami Gardens, with the first public practice Sunday, Aug. 2.
MIA.biggestUnknown: The wide receiver room. With Hill and Waddle both gone and no replacement carrying guaranteed money or first-round capital, Miami genuinely does not know who its No. 1, No. 2 or No. 3 receiver is — and that uncertainty cascades into every evaluation of Malik Willis. Several outlets called it the most unsettled receiver room in the AFC East, and that reads as accurate rather than hyperbolic.

battles.why: Miami has no returning starter opposite Trader and nobody in the room has meaningful guaranteed money or draft capital — it is a career special-teamer, a journeyman, a fifth-round rookie and a UDFA all starting from zero.
battles.stakes: Hafley's defense leans on two-high structures and interchangeable safeties; whoever wins is on the field for most of the snaps in a scheme built around post-safety discipline.
battles.money: No one here is protected: Anderson and Johnson are veteran-minimum types, Taaffe was a 2026 fifth-round pick (Texas), Moore is an undrafted rookie from Indiana. Zero guaranteed money argues the job is truly won on the grass. Anderson's edge is scheme familiarity from Hafley's Green Bay years, not contract.
battles.reportedAs: S2 (free safety, opposite Dante Trader Jr.)

battles.why: Savaiinaea struggled at left guard as a rookie in 2025 and is sliding back to his natural right side, and the new staff has publicly committed to open competition everywhere.
battles.stakes: Miami is pivoting to a heavier, possession-style run game; the right guard/right tackle pairing is where that identity either works or doesn't.
battles.money: Savaiinaea was a 2025 second-round pick on a four-year rookie deal in his second season — teams almost never bench that capital in August for a sixth-round rookie. Campbell (2026 sixth round) is the pressure, not the favorite. Treat the reps as development, not a real coin flip.

MIN.name: Vikings
MIN.campOpens: Rookies reported July 26, 2026; veterans report July 28 at the TCO Performance Center in Eagan. Practices reported to run Aug. 1–20, with joint practices against Baltimore beginning Aug. 19 and a preseason game Aug. 22.
MIN.biggestUnknown: The quarterback. Not just who starts Week 1, but whether J.J. McCarthy — the No. 10 overall pick in 2024 — is the Vikings' future at all. A Murray win doesn't just set a lineup; it triggers trade speculation on McCarthy and reframes the entire roster as win-now. Everything else on this roster is a snap-share question. This one is an identity question.

battles.why: Minnesota passed on the top free-agent centers and didn't draft one until the seventh round, and O'Connell has said publicly he believes Brandel can handle the snaps, protection and line calls after filling in there last season.
battles.stakes: The pivot in a wide-zone offense with a possibly mobile QB; a bad answer here undermines an otherwise strong line of Fries and Jackson at guard.
battles.money: The lack of investment IS the tell: no free-agent center signed, a seventh-round pick (Gerhardt) as the only draft addition, plus an explicit coach endorsement of Brandel. Gerhardt and Jurgens are competing for the backup job, not the starting one. Treat 'center battle' headlines skeptically. Separately, Will Fries is entering a pivotal year with a cap hit that jumps after this season — the real OL decision is 2027, not camp.

NE.name: Patriots
NE.campOpens: Veterans reported Friday, July 24, 2026 (final group); first public practice Saturday, July 25 at 10:30 a.m. at Gillette Stadium — 67th Patriots camp, 24th straight at Gillette, 13 free public practices running July 25 through Aug. 20.
NE.biggestUnknown: The edge rush. New England has no proven double-digit-sack player, Harold Landry opened camp on PUP, and the one high-capital answer — 2026 second-rounder Gabe Jacas — was reported unsigned and missing installs on the eve of camp. Running a close second as an off-field unknown: whether Christian Gonzalez is present and extended, which ESPN made the headline question of its camp preview.

battles.why: Antonio Gibson's departure vacated the third back spot, and incumbent Terrell Jennings opens camp on the active/NFI list — the door is literally open.
battles.stakes: Low ceiling, real floor: Stevenson and Henderson are the offense, so RB3 is a special-teams and injury-insurance job.
battles.money: Nobody here has meaningful guarantees. Jam Miller is a 2026 seventh-rounder and Montgomery is undrafted — the lowest-capital battle on the roster, which is exactly why it's real.

battles.why: Campbell, Moses and Lomu occupy three tackle spots; the fourth is genuinely unclaimed heading into camp.
battles.stakes: With Moses on a managed rep plan at age-cliff range, the swing tackle is closer to snaps than the label suggests.
battles.money: Campbell (No. 4 overall, 2025) and Lomu (No. 28, 2026) are untouchable on capital alone; the competition is strictly for the spot behind them.

battles.why: Lomu is taking heavy first-team RT reps in camp, but only because the staff is deliberately managing Moses' workload — not because the job is open.
battles.stakes: Protects Drake Maye's right side; the real question is when Lomu takes over, not whether.
battles.money: Mike Vrabel publicly outlined the Moses plan and called him the starter; Moses is on a three-year Patriots deal. Lomu was the No. 28 overall pick in 2026 and is explicitly being groomed as the successor — first-round capital means he gets the job on the team's timeline, not camp's.

NYJ.name: Jets
NYJ.campOpens: unknown — could not verify an NYJ-specific report date. No news source was reachable this session.
NYJ.biggestUnknown: Quarterback, and not for Week 1 — the Jets' entire QB room carries roughly $5M in total guarantees (Geno Smith 1yr/$3.3M fully guaranteed, Cade Klubnik a 4th-round rookie at $1.2M guaranteed, Brady Cook and Bailey Zappe on nothing), and no quarterback is under meaningful contract past this season. Geno has held ESPN's QB1 slot for all 127 days without a single flip, so the September starter is fairly clear; what is completely unsettled is whether this is a bridge to Klubnik or a placeholder for a 2027 pick. In a rebuild that just spent the #2 overall pick on a defensive end rather than a quarterback, that is the defining open question on the roster.

battles.why: Geno Smith is on a 1yr/$3.3M deal, which is the kind of number that normally signals a placeholder, and the Jets drafted Klubnik in April — so this will be written as a battle all camp.
battles.stakes: Whether the Jets spend 2026 evaluating a rookie or running out a veteran bridge determines where they pick in 2027.
battles.money: The settling force here is the challenger's lack of capital, not the incumbent's money. Cade Klubnik went in the 4th round (#110) with $1.22M guaranteed — the Jets held three first-round picks and used them on David Bailey, Kenyon Sadiq and Omar Cooper Jr. rather than a quarterback. A team that declined to spend real capital at the position is not handing the job to a Day 3 rookie in August. ESPN has not moved Geno off QB1 once in 127 days; the only movement was Klubnik passing Brady Cook for QB2 on 29 May.

battles.why: The slot job changed hands three separate times in a two-week window (29 May, 2 June, 12 June) between Ponds and Brownlee, the most volatile slot on the roster and the last one to move before the chart froze.
battles.stakes: It is tangled with the outside CB2 question — where Ponds lands determines who plays the other two coverage jobs, so one decision settles three spots.
battles.money: Ponds is a 2026 second-rounder (#50) with $8.95M guaranteed, Brownlee a 2024 fifth-rounder (#146) with $342K guaranteed playing out a rookie deal. Draft capital says Ponds starts somewhere; it does not say where. Genuinely open as to position, close to settled as to whether Ponds plays.

battles.why: The Jets traded Sauce Gardner to Indianapolis and never replaced him with a paid outside corner, leaving one boundary job open to five players who have all held a top-two slot on ESPN's chart at some point since March.
battles.stakes: It is the single largest hole created by the teardown; the Jets are asking a $3.5M free agent or an unproven young pick to cover the spot an All-Pro just vacated.
battles.money: Brandon Stephens (3yr/$36M, $22.98M guaranteed) is locked into the other boundary spot and is not part of this. Nobody competing for the second spot has money that decides anything: Nahshon Wright's 1yr/$3.5M fully guaranteed is the largest figure in the group, Azareye'h Thomas is a 2025 third-rounder (#73) with only $1.44M guaranteed, Tre Brown has $0 guaranteed, Qwan'tez Stiggers has $254K. D'Angelo Ponds (2026 R2, #50, $8.95M of $9.84M guaranteed) has by far the most capital of the challengers, which is why he is more likely to end up somewhere on the field than any of the others.

PHI.name: Eagles
PHI.biggestUnknown: The second safety spot next to Andrew Mukuba, and the knock-on question of where Cooper DeJean actually lines up. Reed Blankenship left for Houston (3yr/$24.75M, $16.5M gtd) and Sydney Brown is off the roster, leaving Marcus Epps — a 39%-snap rotational safety in 2025 on a 1yr/$1.55M deal with $125K guaranteed — nominally holding a starting job. That is the only spot on the roster where the listed starter has essentially no money and no draft capital behind him, and the answer determines whether Michael Carter II (1yr/$2.765M, $1.45M gtd) inherits the nickel.

battles.why: A.J. Brown was traded to New England in early June, vacating a huge target share; the Eagles replaced him with a first-round rookie plus three separate one-year veteran fliers, and the public depth chart has re-sorted WR2 through WR9 twice since (2 June and 21 July) — the most churn anywhere on this roster.
battles.stakes: With Dallas Goedert on a one-year deal and Saquon Barkley aging, the WR3 job is the third-most-targeted skill role in a Jalen Hurts offense that just lost its alpha receiver.
battles.money: Dontayvion Wicks: 1yr/$10.25M, $9M guaranteed — nearly 2x Marquise Brown's 1yr/$5M ($5M gtd) and far above Elijah Moore (1yr/$1.315M, $0 guaranteed). The money leans hard toward Wicks, so treat this as genuine only for the WR4/WR5 order; WR3 itself is probably Wicks. Note that WR2 is NOT open — see the Lemon entry in notes.
battles.reportedAs: WR3 (behind DeVonta Smith and Makai Lemon)

battles.why: Steen is in the final year of his rookie deal with no extension, which perennially generates a 'can he hold the job' storyline in Philadelphia — but he took 96% of the offensive snaps across 18 games in 2025 and nobody behind him is funded.
battles.stakes: The only non-elite spot on an offensive line where the other four starters (Mailata $41M gtd, Dickerson $28.9M gtd, Jurgens $23.3M gtd, Lane Johnson $25M gtd) are all locked in.
battles.money: Steen (2023 R3, #65) has just $1.18M guaranteed left, which is what fuels the storyline — but his challengers have less than nothing: Hollin Pierce $0 guaranteed, Jaeden Roberts $20K guaranteed, Micah Morris (2026 R6, #207) $256K guaranteed, Willie Lampkin $30K guaranteed. A 96%-snap incumbent does not lose to a room of UDFA-money backups. The RG2 flip ESPN logged on 14 May was a backup shuffle, not a threat to the starter.

battles.why: Reed Blankenship signed with Houston and Sydney Brown is gone, leaving no funded starter next to Mukuba; ESPN's chart shuffled the entire SS2-SS4 stack on 23 May and the nominal SS1 has $125K guaranteed.
battles.stakes: Whether Philadelphia can keep Cooper DeJean in the slot — moving him to safety solves one hole by opening another, and forces a $2.7M journeyman into full-time nickel snaps against the NFC East's slot receivers.
battles.money: Marcus Epps: 1yr/$1.55M, only $125K guaranteed, and played just 39% of defensive snaps in 13 games in 2025 — that is a placeholder contract, not a starter's. Mukuba (2025 R2, #64) is locked at FS. DeJean (2024 R2, #40) played 98% of defensive snaps in 2025, so he plays somewhere regardless. Blankenship's departure (3yr/$24.75M, $16.5M gtd to HOU) is the cause of the vacancy.

battles.money: Steen (2023 R3, #65) has just $1.18M guaranteed left, which is what fuels the storyline — but his challengers have less than nothing: Hollin Pierce $0 guaranteed, Jaeden Roberts $20K guaranteed, Micah Morris (2026 R6, #207) $256K guaranteed, Willie Lampkin $30K guaranteed. A 96%-snap incumbent does not lose to a room of UDFA-money backups. The RG2 flip ESPN logged on 14 May was a backup shuffle, not a threat to the starter.

battles.why: A.J. Brown was traded to New England in early June, vacating a huge target share; the Eagles replaced him with a first-round rookie plus three separate one-year veteran fliers, and the public depth chart has re-sorted WR2 through WR9 twice since (2 June and 21 July) — the most churn anywhere on this roster.
battles.stakes: With Dallas Goedert on a one-year deal and Saquon Barkley aging, the WR3 job is the third-most-targeted skill role in a Jalen Hurts offense that just lost its alpha receiver.
battles.money: Dontayvion Wicks: 1yr/$10.25M, $9M guaranteed — nearly 2x Marquise Brown's 1yr/$5M ($5M gtd) and far above Elijah Moore (1yr/$1.315M, $0 guaranteed). The money leans hard toward Wicks, so treat this as genuine only for the WR4/WR5 order; WR3 itself is probably Wicks. Note that WR2 is NOT open — see the Lemon entry in notes.
battles.reportedAs: WR3 (behind DeVonta Smith and Makai Lemon)

battles.why: Five backs and a returner-specialist are stacked in the same room with no separation, and returner was the single churniest slot type league-wide this offseason (7 KR and 6 PR changes post-draft, versus 3 QB changes across all 32 teams).
battles.stakes: Under the dynamic kickoff, returner is now a real field-position lever rather than a roster afterthought — and for Shipley, Bigsby, Mitchell and Pierce it is likely the difference between making the 53 and not.
battles.money: Nobody in this group has leverage: Covey 2yr/$2.315M with $0 guaranteed, Elijah Mitchell 1yr/$1.215M with $0 guaranteed, Dameon Pierce 1yr/$1.29M with $250K guaranteed, Shipley (2024 R4) $717K remaining guaranteed. When no contender has guaranteed money, the competition is real by default.

SEA.name: Seahawks
SEA.campOpens: unknown — no Seahawks-specific reporting was reachable this session. Context: 22 of 32 teams in the local research set report veterans Tuesday July 28, 2026, so that is the overwhelming league default, but I could not confirm Seattle's date and am not going to state one I did not verify.
SEA.biggestUnknown: The back end of the secondary. Seattle lost Riq Woolen, Coby Bryant and Quandre Diggs in one offseason and replaced them with a 2026 second-rounder (Bud Clark, pick 64), a third-rounder (Julian Neal, pick 99), one $8M-per-year corner signing (Josh Jobe, 3yr/$24M) and a returning undrafted starter (Ty Okada, 59% of defensive snaps). Devon Witherspoon and Julian Love are fixed; literally every other coverage snap is up for grabs, and it is the only unit on a Super Bowl-winning roster where the projected personnel is materially worse on paper than what won the title.

battles.why: ESPN's depth chart has flipped Kupp and Shaheed at the WR2 slot during the offseason, and Kupp out-snapped Shaheed 76% to 49% in 2025 (Shaheed arrived midseason).
battles.stakes: Second target share behind Jaxon Smith-Njigba on the league's champion offense.
battles.money: This is the cleanest money read on the roster. Seattle gave Shaheed 3yr/$51M with $23M guaranteed this offseason. Kupp is 33, in year two of a 3yr/$45M signed in 2025 whose $17.5M guarantee is largely earned out. Fresh guarantees beat old ones. Jaxon Smith-Njigba (4yr/$168.6M, $69.13M gtd, signed 2026) makes WR1 a non-question.

battles.why: Kenneth Walker III left for Kansas City after taking 49% of the offensive snaps in 2025, and Seattle spent the 32nd pick — the last of round one, theirs by winning Super Bowl LX — on Jadarian Price to replace him.
battles.stakes: Seattle ran a true 50/50 committee during the title run (Walker 49%, Charbonnet 46%); whoever wins the vacated half inherits roughly 200 touches on the reigning champion's offense.
battles.money: Price signed a 4yr/$16.78M rookie deal that is 100% guaranteed ($4.20M APY) — first-round backs essentially never lose camp battles outright. Charbonnet is a 2023 second-rounder entering the final year of his rookie contract with no extension on file, so Seattle has every financial incentive to find out what Price is.

battles.why: ESPN flipped Egbuka ahead of Godwin on 21 July -- the only change to any Tampa Bay rank-1 slot since April, and precisely the kind of move that generates a week of content.
battles.stakes: Nothing on the roster. Both start in three-receiver sets. It is a target-share question wearing a depth-chart battle's clothes.
battles.money: Godwin reportedly signed a three-year deal in March 2025 with roughly $44M guaranteed; Egbuka was the No. 19 pick in 2025. Two players with that much money and capital both play. Nobody loses a job here -- the ordinal label is cosmetic, and the flip is a public chart reordering itself, not competition.

battles.why: Returner is the most-churned slot class on the public depth chart league-wide this offseason, and Tampa's is live: KR1 flipped from Kameron Johnson to Gainwell on 2 May, with KR2 and KR3 flipping three more times through mid-May.
battles.stakes: Under the current kickoff rules return field position is a real margin, and this is the likeliest path onto the 53 for Kameron Johnson or Tez Johnson.
battles.money: No contender carries meaningful guarantees or premium draft capital -- Gainwell is a veteran addition, the rest are late-round or UDFA-tier. Nothing pre-decides it, which is the whole point: the genuinely open jobs on this roster are the ones nobody writes about.

WAS.name: Commanders
WAS.campOpens: unknown — could not confirm a reported report date; no beat reporting was reachable this session. Camp site is the OrthoVirginia Training Center at Commanders Park, Ashburn, VA (per the repo's camp.json venue field).
WAS.biggestUnknown: The off-ball linebacker room behind Frankie Luvu — specifically who the third linebacker is and who inherits the communication role. Five of Washington's 16 unstable depth-chart slots sit at LILB/RILB, more than double any other position group on the roster, and the instability runs from the starter designation all the way down to LB4. Everything else that moved was WR/RB/CB depth or backup interior offensive line.

battles.why: This is the only Washington slot that registered in the league-wide "movers" table over the 22 Jun - 27 Jul window: Antonio Williams climbed from WR3 to WR2 (z=+0.73) while Luke McCaffrey slid the other way (z=-0.68), meaning the outside view actively changed its mind here rather than merely listing two names.
battles.stakes: The No. 2 target share in a Jayden Daniels offense — the difference between a real weekly role and WR4 rotation snaps.
battles.money: Neither player has guarantees that end a competition. McCaffrey is 2024 third-round capital (Rice, pick ~100) — real but two years stale and not decisive. Williams is late-round/UDFA-tier capital, which is exactly the profile that wins camp jobs outright. Nothing here is bought.

battles.why: RB3, RB4 and RB5 all flipped, with the three names cycling through each other's slots — but RB1 and RB2 never moved once, so the top of the room is stable and the churn is entirely about the back end.
battles.stakes: One of these three likely does not make the 53. Whoever wins it is the change-of-pace/pass-protection back and the injury insurance behind a young lead back.
battles.money: Kaytron Allen is 2026 draft capital, which makes him very hard to cut in Year 1 — that is the one thumb on the scale here. Ford is a veteran free-agent add on what is almost certainly a short, low-guarantee deal; McNichols is veteran-minimum special-teams value. Draft capital probably protects Allen; Ford and McNichols are competing for what's left.
battles.reportedAs: RB3 (backup running back / final RB roster spot)

battles.why: LCB3 flipped twice and LCB4 once, the second-most-volatile cluster on the roster — but CB1 and CB2 never moved, so this is a depth and roster-count fight, not a starting competition.
battles.stakes: The fifth corner and the dime/special-teams role; realistically one roster spot between a rookie and two journeymen.
battles.money: Vigers is a 2026 draft pick, and drafted rookies almost never lose these outright in Year 1 — that alone makes him the favorite regardless of camp reps. Hawkins is 2023 sixth-round capital now in a contract year, Hamilton Sr. is a veteran-minimum journeyman with no protection at all. Genuinely open, but the capital points one way.

battles.why: The LILB1 slot flipped between Luvu and Chenal during the window, which reads as a starting-job battle in a depth chart but is almost certainly the outside view shuffling which side of the formation each man is listed on.
battles.stakes: Who wears the green dot and calls the defense matters; whether both play is not in question.
battles.money: This is the money case. Luvu signed a three-year deal worth roughly $31.5M with about $19M guaranteed in March 2024 and has been the defense's most-used off-ball linebacker since. Chenal arrived as a 2026 free-agent signing — teams do not pay for a linebacker in March and then bench him in July. Two paid starters, two starting jobs. Treat any "Luvu vs Chenal" framing as noise.

battles.why: Five of Washington's 16 flipped slots are off-ball linebacker, and the churn is concentrated at ranks 2-4 (LILB2, LILB3, LILB4, RILB2) — the third-linebacker and special-teams-core spots behind the two paid starters flipped repeatedly across the window.
battles.stakes: In a defense that plays real base snaps, LB3 is a rotational job plus the special-teams captaincy; it is also where two of the last three linebacker draft picks either stick or become cut candidates.
battles.money: No guaranteed money anywhere in this group. Magee is 2024 fifth-round capital, Medrano 2025 sixth-round capital — late-Day-3 picks are the least protected players on any roster. Bellore is a veteran-minimum special-teams specialist. Nothing has been decided by contract.
